subproblem.title: Operator norm bounded by the Hilbert–Schmidt norm
subproblem.statement: For every P ∈ ℕ, every (continuous) linear map A : ℝ^P → ℝ^P (Lean: A : Euclid P →L[ℝ] Euclid P; every linear map on ℝ^P is continuous) and every v ∈ ℝ^P: |Av|² ≤ (Σ_{i=1}^{P} |A e_i|²)·|v|², where e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1 is the standard basis; equivalently the operator norm is bounded by the Hilbert–Schmidt norm, ‖A‖ ≤ |A| := (Σ_i |A e_i|²)^{1/2}.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (A : Euclid P →L[ℝ] Euclid P) (v : Euclid P), ‖A v‖ ^ 2 ≤ (∑ i : Fin P, ‖A (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ))‖ ^ 2) * ‖v‖ ^ 2
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof step 3, the inequality ‖p_x − p_S‖ ≤ |p_x − p_S| (operator norm ≤ Hilbert–Schmidt norm) used for the cross term.

1. Write v = Σ_i v_i e_i with v_i := v(i) the coordinates of v (expansion in the orthonormal basis EuclideanSpace.basisFun); then |v|² = Σ_i v_i² (EuclideanSpace.norm_sq_eq).
2. By linearity Av = Σ_i v_i A e_i, so the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm give |Av| ≤ Σ_i |v_i|·|A e_i|.
3. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for finite sums, (Σ_i |v_i|·|A e_i|)² ≤ (Σ_i |v_i|²)(Σ_i |A e_i|²) = |v|²·Σ_i |A e_i|².
4. Both sides of the inequality in step 2 are nonnegative, so squaring it and using step 3: |Av|² ≤ (Σ_i |v_i|·|A e_i|)² ≤ (Σ_i |A e_i|²)·|v|². ∎

subproblem.title: Projection trace identity trace(p_T(I − p_S)) = ½|p_T − p_S|²
subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ and let T, S be linear subspaces of ℝ^P with dim T = dim S; let p_T, p_S be the orthogonal projections onto T and S (Submodule.starProjection), I the identity and e_1, …, e_P the standard basis (EuclideanSpace.single i 1). Then trace(p_T ∘ (I − p_S)) = ½ Σ_{i=1}^{P} |p_T e_i − p_S e_i|², i.e. trace(p_T(I − p_S)) = ½|p_T − p_S|² for the Hilbert–Schmidt norm.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (T S : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), Module.finrank ℝ T = Module.finrank ℝ S → LinearMap.trace ℝ (Euclid P) (T.starProjection.toLinearMap ∘ₗ (ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ (Euclid P) - S.starProjection).toLinearMap) = 1 / 2 * ∑ i : Fin P, ‖T.starProjection (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ)) - S.starProjection (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ))‖ ^ 2
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof step 3, first identity (Simon, proof of Ch. 5, Lemma 2.1, display (2): Σ_{i>n} e^{ii} = ½Σ_{i,j}(e^{ij} − ε^{ij})² = ½|p_{T_xM} − p_{ℝⁿ}|², which uses e^{ij} = e^{ji}, e² = e and trace e = n; book/chapter-05.txt, lines 236–245). Let p := p_T, s := p_S and m := dim T = dim S.

1. p and s are symmetric (⟨pu, v⟩ = ⟨u, pv⟩, ⟨su, v⟩ = ⟨u, sv⟩ for all u, v) and idempotent (p∘p = p, s∘s = s); these are the defining properties of orthogonal projections (Mathlib: Submodule.inner_starProjection_left_eq_right, Submodule.isIdempotentElem_starProjection).
2. trace p = dim T and trace s = dim S. Indeed p = ι∘π, where π : ℝ^P → T is the orthogonal projection onto T and ι : T → ℝ^P the inclusion; by cyclicity of the trace, trace(ι∘π) = trace(π∘ι) = trace(id_T) = dim T, because π∘ι = id_T. The same argument applies to s.
3. For every linear A on ℝ^P, trace A = Σ_i ⟨e_i, A e_i⟩, because (e_i) is an orthonormal basis (Mathlib: LinearMap.trace_eq_sum_inner with EuclideanSpace.basisFun, whose i-th vector is EuclideanSpace.single i 1).
4. Put D := p − s. By step 1, D is symmetric, so for every i, ‖p e_i − s e_i‖² = ⟨D e_i, D e_i⟩ = ⟨e_i, D(D e_i)⟩. Summing and using step 3: Σ_i ‖p e_i − s e_i‖² = trace(D∘D).
5. By step 1, D∘D = p∘p − p∘s − s∘p + s∘s = p + s − p∘s − s∘p. By linearity of the trace, cyclicity trace(s∘p) = trace(p∘s), and step 2: trace(D∘D) = dim T + dim S − 2 trace(p∘s) = 2m − 2 trace(p∘s) (here dim T = dim S = m is used).
6. Since p∘(I − s) = p − p∘s, step 2 gives trace(p∘(I − s)) = m − trace(p∘s).
7. Steps 4–6 give Σ_i ‖p e_i − s e_i‖² = 2m − 2 trace(p∘s) = 2 trace(p∘(I − s)); dividing by 2 yields trace(p_T∘(I − p_S)) = ½ Σ_i |p_T e_i − p_S e_i|². ∎

subproblem.title: C¹ radial cut-off with |Dζ| ≤ 3/r (cut-off of Simon 5.2.1)
subproblem.statement: For every P ∈ ℕ, every ξ ∈ ℝ^P and every r > 0 there is ζ : ℝ^P → ℝ of class C¹ such that 0 ≤ ζ(x) ≤ 1 for all x, ζ(x) = 1 for every x in the closed ball B̄_{r/2}(ξ), tsupport ζ (the closure of {ζ ≠ 0}) is contained in the closed ball B̄_r(ξ), and the operator norm of the Fréchet derivative satisfies ‖Dζ(x)‖ ≤ 3/r for every x ∈ ℝ^P (Lean: ‖fderiv ℝ ζ x‖ ≤ 3 / r; ℝ^P = Euclid P).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (ξ : Euclid P) (r : ℝ), 0 < r → ∃ ζ : Euclid P → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 ζ ∧ (∀ x, 0 ≤ ζ x ∧ ζ x ≤ 1) ∧ (∀ x ∈ closedBall ξ (r / 2), ζ x = 1) ∧ tsupport ζ ⊆ closedBall ξ r ∧ ∀ x, ‖fderiv ℝ ζ x‖ ≤ 3 / r
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof step 1 (the cut-off), i.e. the choice "ζ ≡ 1 in B_{ρ/2}(0), ζ ≡ 0 outside B_ρ(0) and |∇ζ| ≤ 3/ρ" at the end of Simon's proof of Ch. 5, Lemma 2.1 (book/chapter-05.txt, lines 260–262). Notation: ‖·‖ is the Euclidean norm, B̆ an open ball, B̄ a closed ball.

1. Admissible profiles. Call χ : ℝ → ℝ admissible if (χ1) χ is C¹ (or smoother); (χ2) 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1; (χ3) χ(σ) = 1 for σ ≤ 1/2; (χ4) χ(σ) = 0 for σ ≥ 1; (χ5) |χ(σ) − χ(τ)| ≤ 3|σ − τ| for all σ, τ ∈ ℝ.
2. An admissible profile exists (the cubic of the parent proof). Let χ₀(u) := 1 − 3u² + 2u³. Then χ₀(0) = 1, χ₀(1) = 0 and χ₀'(u) = −6u(1 − u), so χ₀'(0) = χ₀'(1) = 0, χ₀ is nonincreasing on [0, 1] (hence 0 ≤ χ₀ ≤ 1 there) and |χ₀'(u)| = 6u(1 − u) ≤ 3/2 on [0, 1]. Put χ(σ) := 1 for σ ≤ 1/2, χ(σ) := χ₀(2σ − 1) for 1/2 ≤ σ ≤ 1, χ(σ) := 0 for σ ≥ 1 (the definitions agree at σ = 1/2 and σ = 1). On each of the open intervals (−∞, 1/2), (1/2, 1), (1, ∞) χ is a polynomial with derivative 0, 2χ₀'(2σ − 1), 0 respectively. At σ = 1/2 the left difference quotients vanish and (χ(1/2 + h) − 1)/h = −12h + 16h² → 0 as h ↓ 0; at σ = 1 the right difference quotients vanish and (χ(1 − h) − 0)/(−h) = −12h + 16h² → 0 as h ↓ 0. Hence χ is differentiable on ℝ with χ'(σ) = 2χ₀'(2σ − 1) = −12(2σ − 1)(2 − 2σ) for σ ∈ [1/2, 1] and χ'(σ) = 0 otherwise; χ' is continuous (it vanishes at both junctions), so χ is C¹, and |χ'| ≤ 2 · 3/2 = 3. Thus (χ1)–(χ4) hold, and (χ5) follows from |χ'| ≤ 3 by the mean value theorem.
   Remark (an alternative admissible profile, C^∞; it is the one used in the Lean appendix). Let S = Real.smoothTransition (C^∞, 0 ≤ S ≤ 1, S = 0 on (−∞, 0], S = 1 on [1, ∞)) and g(t) := S(12(t − 1/2))·S(12(1 − t)). Then g is C^∞, 0 ≤ g ≤ 1, g = 0 for t ≤ 1/2 and for t ≥ 1, and g = 1 on [7/12, 11/12], so c := ∫_{1/2}^{1} g ≥ 1/3 > 0. Put χ(σ) := 1 − c⁻¹∫_{1/2}^{σ} g. By the fundamental theorem of calculus χ is C^∞ with χ' = −c⁻¹g, so |χ'| ≤ c⁻¹ ≤ 3 and χ is 3-Lipschitz; χ = 1 on (−∞, 1/2], χ = 0 on [1, ∞) (as ∫_{1/2}^{σ} g = c for σ ≥ 1), and 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1 because 0 ≤ ∫_{1/2}^{σ} g ≤ c.
3. Definition. Fix an admissible χ and put ζ(x) := χ(‖x − ξ‖/r).
4. Values and plateau. 0 ≤ ζ ≤ 1 by (χ2). If x ∈ B̄_{r/2}(ξ) then ‖x − ξ‖/r ≤ 1/2, so ζ(x) = 1 by (χ3).
5. Support. If ‖x − ξ‖ ≥ r then ‖x − ξ‖/r ≥ 1 and ζ(x) = 0 by (χ4). Hence {ζ ≠ 0} ⊆ B̆_r(ξ), and tsupport ζ = closure{ζ ≠ 0} ⊆ closure B̆_r(ξ) ⊆ B̄_r(ξ), the closed ball being closed.
6. ζ is C¹. The open sets O₁ := B̆_{r/2}(ξ) and O₂ := ℝ^P \ {ξ} cover ℝ^P (ξ ∈ O₁ because r > 0). On O₁, ζ ≡ 1 by step 4, so ζ is C¹ near every point of O₁. On O₂ the map y ↦ ‖y − ξ‖/r is C^∞ (the Euclidean norm is smooth on ℝ^P \ {0}), so ζ = χ ∘ (‖· − ξ‖/r) is C¹ near every point of O₂ by the chain rule. Being C¹ is a local property, so ζ is C¹ on ℝ^P (C^∞ if χ is C^∞).
7. Gradient bound. For y, z ∈ ℝ^P, (χ5) and the reverse triangle inequality give |ζ(y) − ζ(z)| ≤ (3/r)·|‖y − ξ‖ − ‖z − ξ‖| ≤ (3/r)·‖y − z‖, so ζ is (3/r)-Lipschitz. For every x and h, |Dζ(x)h| = lim_{t↓0} |ζ(x + th) − ζ(x)|/t ≤ (3/r)‖h‖, i.e. ‖Dζ(x)‖ ≤ 3/r (Mathlib: norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz).
8. Steps 4–7 give all assertions. (For P = 0 the space is {ξ} ⊆ O₁ and everything is immediate.) ∎

subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let T, S be linear subspaces of ℝ^P with orthogonal projections p_T, p_S, let ξ, x ∈ ℝ^P, and let ζ : ℝ^P → ℝ be differentiable at x. Put X(y) := ζ(y)²·((y − ξ) − p_S(y − ξ)). Then trace(p_T ∘ DX(x)) = ζ(x)²·trace(p_T ∘ (I − p_S)) + 2ζ(x)·Dζ(x)[p_T((x − ξ) − p_S(x − ξ))], where DX(x) = fderiv ℝ X x and Dζ(x) = fderiv ℝ ζ x. For T = T_xM = approxTangentPlane n M x the left side is tangentialDivergence n M X x = div_M X(x).

Source: parent proof step 2 (Simon, proof of Ch. 5, Lemma 2.1: the test field X = ζ²(x)x′ and the computation of div_M X, book/chapter-05.txt, lines 222–247). Write q := I − p_S (a continuous linear map) and w(y) := (y − ξ) − p_S(y − ξ) = q(y − ξ).

1. w is affine, w(y) = q(y) − q(ξ), hence differentiable at every point with Dw(x) = q.
2. g(y) := ζ(y)² is differentiable at x with Dg(x) = 2ζ(x)·Dζ(x) (chain rule for t ↦ t²).
3. Product rule for a scalar function times a vector function: X = g·w is differentiable at x and, for every h ∈ ℝ^P, DX(x)h = g(x)·Dw(x)h + (Dg(x)h)·w(x) = ζ(x)² q h + 2ζ(x)(Dζ(x)h)·w(x). In operator form DX(x) = ζ(x)²·q + (2ζ(x)Dζ(x)) ⊗ w(x), where (L ⊗ u)(h) := L(h)u is the rank-one map (Mathlib: ContinuousLinearMap.smulRight). As X is differentiable at x, fderiv ℝ X x is this operator.

1. κ ≥ 0, since 0 ≤ |H(0)| ≤ κ.
2. μ(K) < ∞. K is compact (ζ has compact support), closed hence Borel, and K ⊆ W ⊆ U. By the definitions of withDensity and of the restricted measure, μ(K) = ∫_{M∩K} θ dHⁿ, which is finite by the field R.locallyIntegrable_mult applied to the compact set K ⊆ U.
3. Integrability criterion. If f : ℝ^P → ℝ is μ-a.e. strongly measurable, |f| ≤ C on ℝ^P and f = 0 outside K, then |f| ≤ C·1_K, and C·1_K is μ-integrable by step 2; hence f is μ-integrable.
4. Elementary bounds. (i) ζ is continuous with compact support, so |ζ| ≤ Z for some Z ≥ 0, and ζ = 0 outside K. (ii) Dζ = fderiv ℝ ζ is continuous (ζ is C¹) and vanishes outside K (a function vanishing on a neighbourhood of a point has zero derivative there, and every point outside tsupport ζ has such a neighbourhood), so ‖Dζ‖ ≤ D′ for some D′ ≥ 0. (iii) w is continuous (affine), so b ≤ B on the compact set K for some B ≥ 0. (iv) 0 ≤ a ≤ 4P everywhere: orthogonal projections have operator norm ≤ 1 and |e_i| = 1, so |p_x e_i − p_S e_i| ≤ |p_x e_i| + |p_S e_i| ≤ 2.
5. Measurability. As x ↦ p_x is μ-a.e. strongly measurable (hypothesis), so is x ↦ p_x e_i (evaluation at a fixed vector is a continuous linear function of the operator), hence a (continuous operations and a finite sum), and so is x ↦ p_x w(x) (the evaluation (A, v) ↦ Av is jointly continuous and w is continuous). ζ, Dζ and w are continuous, and H is μ-a.e. strongly measurable, so x ↦ ⟨X(x), H(x)⟩ is μ-a.e. strongly measurable for every continuous X (the inner product is continuous).

By steps 4–5 each is μ-a.e. strongly measurable and bounded on ℝ^P (|F₁| ≤ 4PZ², |F₂| ≤ 2ZD′B, |F₃| ≤ Z²Bκ, G₁ ≤ D′²B², G₂ ≤ κZ²B, using |p_x w(x)| ≤ |w(x)| ≤ B on K), and each vanishes outside K because it contains the factor ζ or Dζ. 8. First variation as a μ-integral. By definition R.firstVariation X = ∫_M θ·div_M X dHⁿ with div_M X(x) = tangentialDivergence n M X x = trace(p_x∘DX(x)). Since μ = (Hⁿ⌞M).withDensity θ with θ measurable and ℕ-valued (hence ℝ≥0-valued), ∫ g dμ = ∫_M θ·g dHⁿ for every real function g, with no integrability assumption (Mathlib: integral_withDensity_eq_integral_smul). 9. Almost every approximate tangent plane is n-dimensional. By the field R.orients, for Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. x there is Q with HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt n M x Q. At such x, the definition of approxTangentPlane selects some Q′ with HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt n M x Q′, and the first conjunct of that predicate is dim Q′ = n. 10. Pointwise divergence. For every x, ζ is differentiable at x, so (D) with T = T_x gives div_M X(x) = ζ(x)²·trace(p_x∘(I − p_S)) + F₂(x). For μ-a.e. x, dim T_x = n = dim S by step 9, so (B) gives trace(p_x∘(I − p_S)) = ½a(x). Hence div_M X = ½F₁ + F₂ μ-a.e.
11. The identity. By steps 6, 8, 10 and 7 and linearity of the integral on integrable functions: ½∫F₁ dμ + ∫F₂ dμ = ∫(½F₁ + F₂) dμ = ∫div_M X dμ = R.firstVariation X = −∫F₃ dμ.
12. Cross term. Fix x and put L := Dζ(x). Since w(x) = v − p_S v with v := x − ξ lies in S^⊥, p_S w(x) = 0, hence p_x w(x) = (p_x − p_S)w(x). 13. Curvature term. −F₃(x) ≤ |⟨X(x), H(x)⟩| ≤ |X(x)|·|H(x)| = ζ(x)²b(x)|H(x)| ≤ κζ(x)²b(x) = G₂(x).
14. Absorption. Integrating steps 12 and 13 (monotonicity of the integral for integrable functions): −∫F₂ ≤ ¼∫F₁ + 4∫G₁ and −∫F₃ ≤ ∫G₂. With step 11, ½∫F₁ = −∫F₂ − ∫F₃ ≤ ¼∫F₁ + 4∫G₁ + ∫G₂. As ∫F₁ is a finite real number, ¼∫F₁ ≤ 4∫G₁ + ∫G₂, i.e. ∫F₁ ≤ 16∫G₁ + 4∫G₂.
15. Lower integrals. F₁, G₁, G₂ are nonnegative (κ ≥ 0 by step 1) and integrable, so ∫⁻ ofReal(F₁) dμ = ofReal(∫F₁ dμ), and likewise for G₁ and G₂ (Mathlib: ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal). As F₁ = ζ²|p_x − p_S|², G₁ = ‖Dζ‖²|w|² and G₂ = κζ²|w|, this is the assertion. ∎
